subject: physiology
title: Intrapleural Pressure, Transpulmonary Pressure, and Compliance

steps.tx: Ventilatory gas flow into and out of the lungs is powered by cyclic fluctuations in thoracic pressures. The fluid-filled potential space separating the visceral pleura covering the lungs from the parietal pleura lining the thoracic cage maintains **intrapleural pressure**. Under normal resting conditions at end-expiration, intrapleural pressure is subatmospheric, measuring negative five centimetres of water.
steps.say: Intrapleural pressure within the pleural space is normally subatmospheric, measuring negative five centimetres of water at rest due to opposing elastic recoils.

nodes.label: Inward Elastic Recoil of Lung Parenchyma Pulls Visceral Pleura Inward
Outward Elastic Spring of Thoracic Cage Pulls Parietal Pleura Outward
Two Opposing Elastic Forces Generate Subatmospheric Negative Vacuum
Resting Intrapleural Pressure Equals -5 cm H2O at End-Expiration

steps.tx: The subatmospheric resting intrapleural pressure is generated by two opposing mechanical forces: the inward elastic recoil of the lungs pulling inward, opposed by the outward elastic recoil of the compliant thoracic wall springing outward. During active inspiration, contraction of the diaphragm and external intercostals expands thoracic volume, dropping intrapleural pressure to **negative eight** centimetres of water.
steps.say: During inspiration, diaphragmatic descent expands thoracic volume, dropping intrapleural pressure from negative five to negative eight centimetres of water.

left.title: End-Expiration (Resting FRC)
points: Alveolar pressure equals atmospheric pressure (0 cm H2O)
Zero airflow into or out of respiratory tree

right.title: Mid-Inspiration
points: Diaphragm contracts and descends 1 to 2 cm
Intrapleural pressure drops to -8 cm H2O
Alveolar pressure falls to -1 cm H2O (inward gradient)
Inward airflow of 500 mL tidal volume enters lungs

steps.tx: The distending pressure that holds the lungs open against their inward elastic collapse is the **transpulmonary pressure**, defined as alveolar pressure minus intrapleural pressure. Transpulmonary pressure is always positive under physiological conditions: at rest, alveolar pressure (zero) minus intrapleural pressure (negative five) yields a positive distending pressure of plus five centimetres of water.
steps.say: Transpulmonary pressure is alveolar minus intrapleural pressure, normally positive plus five centimetres of water, holding the alveoli open against collapse.

nodes.label: Alveolar Pressure (Palv): 0 cm H2O at End-Expiration
Transpulmonary Pressure (PL = Palv - Pip): +5 cm H2O
Positive Distending Pressure Keeps Alveoli Inflated Against Recoil

steps.tx: The distensibility of the respiratory system is quantified as pulmonary **compliance**, defined as the change in lung volume per unit change in transpulmonary pressure. In a healthy young adult, static lung compliance measures approximately two hundred millilitres per centimetre of water, reflecting the ease with which lungs expand under distending pressure.
steps.say: Pulmonary compliance measures volume expansion per unit change in transpulmonary pressure, normally two hundred millilitres per centimetre of water.

vis.alt: Lung compliance curves and surfactant function in alveoli.
vis.caption: Lung compliance curves and surfactant function in alveoli. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Pulmonary compliance is profoundly altered in parenchymal lung diseases. In pulmonary fibrosis, excessive deposition of stiff collagen in the alveolar interstitium decreases compliance, shifting the pressure-volume curve downward and to the right. Conversely, in **emphysema**, destruction of elastin fibres reduces inward elastic recoil, abnormally increasing compliance and predisposing to dynamic airway collapse.
steps.say: Compliance falls in pulmonary fibrosis due to stiff collagen, but rises in emphysema due to loss of elastic recoil, causing expiratory airway collapse.

left.title: Decreased Compliance (Fibrosis / ARDS)
points: Lungs are stiff, non-compliant, and difficult to inflate
Pressure-volume curve shifts downward and to the right
Markedly elevated work of breathing to expand lungs
Causes: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, infant RDS, oedema

right.title: Increased Compliance (Emphysema)
points: Destruction of alveolar septa and elastin fibers
Pressure-volume curve shifts upward and to the left
Loss of elastic recoil impairs passive expiration
Leads to dynamic small airway collapse and air trapping

steps.tx: Plotting lung volume against transpulmonary pressure during inflation versus deflation reveals that the deflation curve does not retrace the inflation curve, a phenomenon known as **hysteresis**. For any given transpulmonary pressure, lung volume is greater during deflation than during inflation, caused by surface tension forces at the air-liquid interface and recruitment of collapsed alveoli.
steps.say: Hysteresis means lung volume is larger during deflation than inflation at the same pressure, caused by surface tension behavior and alveolar recruitment.

rows: Overcoming surface tension in collapsed alveoli
Surfactant molecules concentrate, lowering surface tension
Demonstrates surface tension accounts for 2/3 of recoil

steps.tx: When air enters the pleural cavity through an open chest wound or rupture of an apical bulla, a **pneumothorax** develops. As atmospheric air rushes down its pressure gradient into the pleural space, intrapleural pressure rises from negative five to zero centimetres of water. With transpulmonary pressure abolished, the inward elastic recoil causes the lung to collapse completely.
steps.say: In pneumothorax, air enters the pleural space, abolishing subatmospheric intrapleural pressure and causing the lung to collapse by its own elastic recoil.

vis.alt: Tension pneumothorax on chest radiograph: hyperlucent hemithorax with collapsed lung.
vis.caption: Tension pneumothorax on chest radiograph: hyperlucent hemithorax with collapsed lung. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: A life-threatening variant is **tension pneumothorax**, where a one-way flap valve allows air to enter the pleural space during inspiration but traps it during expiration. Intrapleural pressure rises above atmospheric, collapsing the lung, shifting the mediastinum and trachea contralaterally, and compressing the vena cava, producing acute obstructive shock treated by immediate needle decompression.
steps.say: Tension pneumothorax traps air under positive pressure, shifting the mediastinum, compressing the vena cava, and causing fatal obstructive shock.

Mediastinum and Trachea Displaced to Contralateral Hemithorax
